newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian prompt naphtha prices surge on Thai buying.
newsitem.headline: Asian prompt naphtha prices surge on Thai buying.

text.p: A flurry of naphtha buying by a Thai petrochemical company has pushed the Asian naphtha market into backwardation, but traders said Friday the bull run would be shortlived.
"The market players were laid back until very recently as they were able to procure cargoes whenever they wanted," a naphtha trader in Japan said.
"The relaxed sentiment is gone with Thailand sweeping the market of prompt Mediterranean cargoes," he said.
Traders said Thailand's Aromatics (Thailand) Plc has bought at least six 30,000-tonne cargoes of full-range naphtha from the Mediterranean for prompt delivery between July 4 and August 2.
The company has purchased naphtha as a temporary measure to replace the use of crude condensate at its 650,000 tonne-per-year petrochemical aromatics plant on the eastern seabord.
It has cut back on condensate use while a unit -- that extracts mercury from condensate -- is shut down for maintenance. The unit is due to shut down from mid July for up to two months.

On Thursday, prices of Japan's open-specification forward contract for second-half August delivery traded $1.50 per tonne higher than second-half September, the first backwardation seen since late April.
On Friday, second-half September was quoted at $203.00/$204.00 per tonne.
An influx of arbitrage cargoes in April, mainly from the Mediterranean, dampened sentiment and pushed the market in contango.
The contango hit a 17-month record in early May when prompt prices were at least $2.50 lower than the next half-month's quotes.
Naphtha in Asia is usually a backwardated market amid a shortfall in the region and growing demand as new plants have come onstream this year, particularly in the petrochemical sector.
Some traders said spreads would stay backwardated if Thailand continued purchasing naphtha instead of condensate as its feedstock.
But others were not optimistic the Thai purchases would support backwardation because only three cargoes have been purchased above normal requirements.
"The only bullish factor is Thailand, and there are still spot avails and the arbitrage window is open," a trader said.
Traders said while Middle East producers were offering spot cargoes to Asia for August, Mediterranean arbitrage cargoes could still arrive in Asia at $4 per tonne below Asian prices.

"It is more psychological than fundamental," said a western trader. "Second-half September/second-half October should go back to flat or even a slight contango. I don't think the Thai buying is the main reason... there is something else going on which I am trying to find out myself."
With contribution from Kiyoshi Takenaka in Tokyo.
